practices.name: Growth & Commercial Strategy
practices.meta_description: Commercial strategy grounded in behavioral science: cross-sell design, messaging research, go-to-market, retention, product strategy and investor diligence.
practices.tagline: Revenue is a series of human decisions. We find them, measure them and design for them.
intro: Every commercial number is the sum of decisions people make: a buyer agreeing to a second meeting, a relationship manager introducing a colleague, a customer renewing instead of drifting away. Most growth plans treat those decisions as volume to be pushed. Our growth and commercial strategy work treats them as behavior to be understood, because behavior can be observed, predicted and improved with far more precision than a forecast built on last year's averages.

We bring behavioral science, process design and data analysis to the moments where revenue is won or lost. That means mapping how deals actually move through a firm, testing which messages change minds, and defining the leading indicators that tell a leadership team whether a strategy is working before the quarter closes. The same lens serves investors, who need to know whether a company's customers and leaders will behave the way the investment thesis assumes.

Our perspective is shaped by practice as much as theory. We have mapped cross-sell processes in commercial real estate capital markets, researched the gap between an industry's real benefits and public perception, and founded and scaled software companies of our own. We know what it takes to turn insight into a pipeline that moves, a product people adopt and a customer base that stays.

themes.title: Decisions, not funnels
themes.body: A funnel describes volume. It rarely explains why a prospect stalls between stages or why a referral never happens. We study the specific decision at each stage, who makes it, what they need to believe and what friction stands in the way, so growth strategy addresses causes rather than symptoms.

themes.title: Leading indicators of revenue
themes.body: Bookings and churn arrive too late to steer by. Using Behavioral Signals Design, we identify the earlier behaviors that predict commercial outcomes, such as handoff speed, multi-product engagement or onboarding milestones, and turn them into predictive KPIs that leaders can manage week to week.

themes.title: Growth that respects people
themes.body: Persuasion works best when it helps customers do what they already want to do. We design offers, messages and processes that reduce confusion and build trust, and we avoid tactics that win a transaction while eroding the relationship. Durable revenue and ethical practice point in the same direction.

practices.name: Social Impact & Public Good
practices.meta_title: Social Impact & Public Good: Behavioral Science
practices.meta_description: Behavioral science for mission-driven organizations: impact strategy, learning design, research translation, public education campaigns and evaluation.
practices.tagline: Behavioral science that helps people get care, learn, understand evidence and live healthier lives.
intro: The public good is made of individual behaviors: a parent scheduling a child's screening, a teenager reaching a counselor before a crisis, a teacher trying a better practice, a clinician adopting new evidence, a resident trusting sound public health guidance. Mission-driven organizations ask for these behaviors every day, with fewer resources than a commercial brand and far higher stakes. This practice brings the same rigor we apply to commercial problems to the work of public health associations, medical associations, academic medicine, school districts and community mental health organizations.

We help these organizations understand the people they serve, translate research into language and tools people can use, design learning experiences grounded in how adults and young people actually learn, and measure whether programs are producing the change they promise. The work draws on health psychology, behavioral medicine, knowledge translation, logic models and evaluation design, all applied with a practical sense of what busy staff and boards can sustain.

This practice also reflects a conviction. Behavioral science should help people do what they already want to do, never manipulate them. That principle extends to how organizations adopt AI, what knowledge gets made accessible and to whom, and which cultures are represented in the training material that will shape future systems. We take those questions seriously because the communities affected by them deserve it.

themes.title: From evidence to everyday practice
themes.body: Good research often stalls before it reaches the clinician, teacher, parent or patient who could use it. We apply knowledge translation and plain-language design to move findings into decisions, materials and routines, so the value of scientific work is measured by what changes in practice, not only by what gets published.

themes.title: Programs built on a theory of change
themes.body: Many programs run for years on good intentions and attendance counts. We help organizations articulate a theory of change and logic model, identify the behaviors that link activities to outcomes, and design evaluation that tells leaders and funders what is working, for whom, and why.

themes.title: Ethical persuasion and responsible AI
themes.body: Public education and digital tools carry real influence over people's choices. We design campaigns and products that respect autonomy, explain rather than pressure, and work for people with different literacy levels and backgrounds. We also help organizations consider whose knowledge and cultures AI systems learn from and what that means for the communities they serve.

services.name: Cross-Sell & Sales Process Design
services.meta_title: Cross-Sell Strategy & Sales Process Design Consulting
services.meta_description: Cross-sell strategy built on behavioral science: map handoffs, find the conversion points that stall referrals, and design sales processes teams will use.
services.summary: Find where referrals and handoffs stall between teams, then redesign the sales process around the behaviors that actually produce multi-product relationships.
services.lede: A cross-sell strategy fails or succeeds in small moments: a banker deciding whether to introduce a colleague, a client deciding whether to take the meeting. We map those moments, measure them and redesign the process around them.
challenge: Most firms with more than one line of business believe their clients should buy more than one thing from them. Leadership sets cross-sell targets, launches incentive plans and builds shared CRM fields. Yet the referrals stay thin. The reasons are rarely about effort. Producers worry that a colleague will mishandle a relationship they spent years building. Clients are not sure what the second service is or why it matters to them now. Credit for the outcome is ambiguous, so the safest choice is to do nothing.

Those are behavioral problems, and a cross-sell strategy that ignores them tends to produce activity without results. In commercial real estate capital markets, for example, we have seen that the decisive moments sit in handoffs between debt, equity, investment sales and servicing teams, where accountability blurs and information gets lost. Until a firm can see which handoffs convert, which stall and why, incentive changes and training programs are educated guesses rather than interventions aimed at a known cause.

approach.title: Shadow the real handoffs
approach.body: We interview producers, analysts and client-facing leaders across each line of business and walk through recent deals end to end. The goal is to see how referrals actually happen, including the informal ones, what people fear when they pass a client along, and which client moments open the door to a second conversation.

approach.title: Measure stage conversion
approach.body: We assemble CRM records, pipeline history and deal data, often from systems that were never integrated, and calculate conversion at each sales stage and handoff. We look for behavioral types among producers and clients, and for the early signals, such as joint meetings or shared pitch materials, that predict whether a cross-sell opportunity closes.

approach.title: Redesign the process and prompts
approach.body: Using swimlane maps, we redesign the sales process so that ownership, timing and information transfer are explicit at every handoff. We design prompts at the moments clients are most receptive, address loss aversion among producers through shared credit rules, and draft talk tracks that explain the second service in the client's terms.

approach.title: Pilot with selected teams
approach.body: We pilot the redesigned process with a few teams or regions and compare them against a matched group. We track the predictive KPIs defined earlier, such as introduction rate and time from referral to first meeting, so leaders can see whether behavior is changing well before revenue figures confirm it.

approach.title: Build it into the operating rhythm
approach.body: Successful changes are written into playbooks, CRM workflows and pipeline reviews. We coach sales leaders to run cross-sell conversations in their regular meetings and build a simple dashboard of leading indicators, so the process keeps improving after the engagement ends rather than fading with the next priority.

deliverables: Current-state swimlane map of cross-team sales handoffs
Stage-by-stage conversion analysis across lines of business
Producer and client behavioral types with referral drivers
Redesigned sales process with explicit ownership at each handoff
Client-facing talk tracks and introduction prompts
Cross-sell leading-indicator dashboard and pilot readout
outcomes: Leaders can see exactly where cross-sell opportunities stall and which handoffs need attention first
Producers trust the referral process because ownership, credit and follow-through are clearly defined
Clients understand why a second service is relevant to them at the moment it is offered
Pipeline reviews track leading indicators of cross-sell rather than waiting for quarterly revenue results
services.who_we_serve: We work with heads of sales, chief revenue officers, managing directors and practice leaders in multi-line firms: commercial real estate capital markets platforms, banks and wealth managers, professional services firms and B2B technology companies. Typical trigger moments include a merger that brought new service lines under one brand, a cross-sell target that keeps being missed, a new CRM rollout, or a strategic plan that depends on deepening existing client relationships rather than winning new ones.
services.impact_lens: Good cross-selling serves clients first. When handoffs are clear, clients get coordinated advice instead of fragmented pitches and spend less time repeating their story to different teams. Employees benefit from a process that protects their relationships and recognizes collaboration fairly, which reduces internal friction and turf conflict. Firms that build trust this way earn deeper relationships honestly, and we deliberately avoid pressure tactics that sell products clients do not need.

faqs.q: Why do cross-sell programs so often underperform?
faqs.a: Most programs focus on targets and incentives while the real barriers are behavioral. Producers fear losing control of a relationship, credit rules are unclear, and clients do not see why the second service matters to them. Handoffs between teams also lose information. A cross-sell strategy that addresses those specific frictions, measured at each stage, tends to outperform one that simply raises the target.

faqs.q: What data do you need to start?
faqs.a: CRM opportunity records and pipeline history are the usual starting point, supplemented by deal or transaction data, billing records and calendar or meeting data where available. The data is rarely clean or integrated, and that is expected. Interviews and deal walkthroughs fill in what the systems miss, and part of our work is identifying which gaps matter enough to fix.

faqs.q: Do you redesign incentive and compensation plans?
faqs.a: We advise on the behavioral effects of incentives, such as how credit-sharing rules affect willingness to refer, and we work with your compensation and finance leaders on changes. We do not treat incentives as the only lever. Process clarity, social proof from respected peers and well-timed prompts often change referral behavior faster and at lower cost than compensation redesign.

faqs.q: How is this different from sales training?
faqs.a: Sales training improves individual skill. Cross-sell process design changes the system people work within: who owns each step, what information moves with the client, when prompts appear and what gets measured. Training can be part of the solution, but it works far better once the process supports the behavior you are training for.

services.name: Brand Messaging Research
services.meta_title: Brand Messaging Research & Message Testing Consulting
services.meta_description: Brand messaging research that tests which framing changes beliefs and behavior, using behavioral science, perception research and controlled message tests.
services.summary: Learn which messages change what your audience believes and does, using perception research, behavioral framing and controlled message testing.
services.lede: Brand messaging research should tell you more than which tagline people like. We study the gap between what your audience believes and what is true, then test which framing actually changes beliefs and behavior.
challenge: Many messaging decisions are made in a conference room. A team debates three headlines, picks the one leadership prefers, and launches. When results disappoint, the explanation is usually creative execution or media spend. The deeper issue is often that nobody established what the audience currently believes, which beliefs are blocking action, and whether the chosen message addresses them at all. Preference surveys add little, because people are poor predictors of what will persuade them.

The gap between an organization's real value and public perception can be wide. We have researched exactly that gap for an industry whose genuine benefits were poorly understood by consumers, in order to ground an education campaign in evidence rather than assumption. That work showed how much depends on framing: whether a benefit is expressed as a gain or an avoided loss, whether it is anchored to something familiar, and whether the messenger is trusted. Small framing choices carry large consequences.

approach.title: Map current beliefs
approach.body: We conduct interviews and open-ended research with target audiences to understand what they believe about your category, your brand and the behavior you want. We pay close attention to the language people use, the misconceptions they hold and the sources they trust, since these shape which messages will land and which will be dismissed.

approach.title: Quantify the perception gap
approach.body: We design a survey that measures beliefs, attitudes and intentions with validated items where possible, then segment respondents by behavior and belief rather than demographics alone. The analysis shows which beliefs most strongly predict the behavior you care about, so messaging targets the beliefs that matter rather than the ones that are easiest to address.

approach.title: Build framed message variants
approach.body: We write message variants that each test a specific hypothesis: gain versus loss framing, social proof, concrete examples versus abstract claims, different messengers and different calls to action. Each variant is tied to a belief identified earlier, so the test produces learning about your audience and not just a winner.

approach.title: Run controlled message tests
approach.body: We run randomized message experiments with online panels, email campaigns or live digital channels, measuring changes in comprehension, belief and stated or observed behavior. Where possible we measure real actions such as click-through, sign-up or inquiry, since these predict market response more reliably than stated preference.

approach.title: Codify the messaging system
approach.body: We translate results into a messaging framework with core claims, proof points, framing guidance and language to avoid, written for the agencies and internal teams who will use it. We also set up an ongoing testing cadence so messaging keeps improving as audiences and markets change.

deliverables: Audience belief map with key misconceptions and trusted sources
Perception gap analysis linking beliefs to behavior
Hypothesis-driven message variants with framing rationale
Randomized message test design and results readout
Messaging framework with claims, proof points and language guidance
Ongoing message testing plan for internal and agency teams
outcomes: Messaging decisions are based on evidence about what changes beliefs, not on internal preference
Teams understand which audience beliefs block action and which messages address them
Agencies receive clear framing guidance grounded in research rather than vague brand adjectives
Campaigns can be tested and refined continuously instead of judged only after launch
services.who_we_serve: We work with chief marketing officers, brand and communications leaders, product marketers and association executives who need to change how a market understands them. Common triggers include a repositioning, a new product category the market does not yet understand, an industry facing negative or outdated perceptions, an upcoming education or awareness campaign, and agency briefs that keep producing work leadership cannot evaluate with confidence.
services.impact_lens: Clear, accurate messaging helps customers make better decisions with less confusion. When an industry's real benefits are misunderstood, people may avoid products or services that would genuinely help them. Our research aims to close that gap honestly, correcting misconceptions without overstating claims. Employees benefit from a story they can tell with conviction, and communities benefit when public understanding rests on evidence rather than marketing noise.

faqs.q: How is brand messaging research different from a focus group?
faqs.a: Focus groups are useful for exploring language and reactions, and we sometimes use them early. But group settings encourage conformity, and stated preferences rarely predict behavior. Brand messaging research combines qualitative exploration with quantitative belief measurement and randomized message tests, so conclusions rest on how people actually respond to framing rather than what they say they prefer.

faqs.q: What does message framing mean in practice?
faqs.a: Framing is how the same fact is presented. A benefit can be described as something gained or a loss avoided, compared to a familiar reference point, attributed to a peer or an expert, or made concrete with an example. Behavioral science shows these choices affect attention, belief and action. We test framing deliberately rather than leaving it to chance.

faqs.q: Can you work with our existing agency?
faqs.a: Yes, and we usually prefer to. Agencies bring creative craft and channel expertise. We bring audience research, behavioral framing and experimental design. Our deliverables are written to be used by agency teams, and we often collaborate on variants so that tested messages are also executable creative. Agencies also gain a stronger basis for defending creative choices with leadership.

faqs.q: Do you measure real behavior or only attitudes?
faqs.a: Both, with a preference for behavior. Attitude and belief measures tell you why a message works. Observed actions, such as clicks, inquiries or sign-ups in a live channel, tell you whether it works. Combining them gives you a messaging system you can trust and keep improving. Behavioral measures also reveal when a message is liked but does not move anyone to act.

services.name: Behavioral Go-to-Market Strategy
services.meta_description: A go-to-market strategy built on how buyers actually decide: jobs to be done, behavioral segments, choice architecture and early tests before full launch.
services.summary: Build a go-to-market strategy around how your buyers actually decide, with behavioral segments, tested offers and leading indicators of traction.
services.lede: A go-to-market strategy rests on assumptions about who will buy, why and how. We turn those assumptions into testable hypotheses, design the launch around real buying behavior, and measure early signals of traction.
challenge: Launch plans are often detailed about channels, pricing tiers and timelines while remaining vague about the buyer's decision. Who feels the problem most acutely? What are they doing today instead? What would they need to believe to switch, and who else has to agree? When those questions are answered by assumption, the plan looks complete on paper but carries hidden risk. The first signal that something is wrong is often a slow quarter, by which point budgets are committed.

Behavioral science offers a better starting point. Jobs-to-be-done research reveals the progress buyers are trying to make. Behavioral segmentation groups prospects by what they do rather than by firmographics alone. Choice architecture shapes how offers, plans and defaults are presented. Status quo bias and loss aversion explain why a clearly superior product can still lose to doing nothing. A go-to-market strategy that accounts for these forces is more likely to find traction quickly and to recognize when it has not.

approach.title: Research the buying decision
approach.body: We conduct jobs-to-be-done interviews with recent buyers, lost prospects and people who chose to do nothing. We reconstruct how each decision unfolded: the triggering event, alternatives considered, who was involved and what nearly stopped them. This reveals the real competition, which is often an existing habit or workaround rather than another vendor.

approach.title: Define behavioral segments
approach.body: Using available CRM, product, web and market data, we identify behavioral segments defined by need, urgency and buying behavior. We look for the early signals that predict a qualified opportunity, such as specific usage patterns, content engagement or trigger events, and define the predictive KPIs that will show whether the launch is gaining traction.

approach.title: Shape the offer and path
approach.body: We design positioning, offers and the buying path for each priority segment. That includes choice architecture for plans and pricing pages, defaults and trial structures, messaging that addresses switching costs and loss aversion, and sales motions matched to how each segment prefers to buy. Every major choice is documented as a hypothesis to test.

approach.title: Run small market tests
approach.body: Before committing the full budget, we run focused tests: landing page and offer experiments, outbound sequences to defined segments, pilot pricing or limited regional launches. We compare results against the hypotheses and adjust segment priorities, messaging and offers based on observed behavior rather than internal enthusiasm.

approach.title: Launch with live instruments
approach.body: We help commercial teams roll out the validated strategy with a dashboard of leading indicators, clear decision rules for when to adjust, and enablement materials grounded in buyer research. Leaders know which signals to watch in the first weeks and what they will do if those signals disappoint.

deliverables: Jobs-to-be-done research synthesis with buyer decision stories
Behavioral segment profiles with priority and sizing rationale
Hypothesis register for positioning, pricing and channel assumptions
Offer, pricing page and buying path designs per segment
Market test plan with results and recommended adjustments
Launch leading-indicator dashboard with decision rules
outcomes: Launch plans rest on tested evidence about buyers rather than untested internal assumptions
Commercial teams focus effort on segments that show genuine need and urgency
Offers and pricing pages make the right choice easier for each buyer type
Leaders spot weak traction early and adjust before budgets are fully committed
services.who_we_serve: We work with founders, chief executives, chief marketing and revenue officers, and product leaders preparing to bring something new to market. Typical moments include a new product or category launch, entry into a new segment or geography, a repositioning after a disappointing launch, a shift from founder-led sales to a scalable sales motion, and portfolio companies whose investment thesis depends on expanding into adjacent markets.
services.impact_lens: A well-researched go-to-market strategy serves buyers by presenting offers they can understand and compare honestly, without confusing tiers or manipulative urgency. Employees benefit when sales and marketing teams pursue buyers who genuinely need the product, which makes their work more rewarding. Organizations conserve resources that would otherwise go to campaigns aimed at the wrong audience, and markets work better when products reach the people they actually help.

faqs.q: What makes a go-to-market strategy behavioral?
faqs.a: A behavioral go-to-market strategy starts from how buyers actually decide rather than from channels and budgets. It uses jobs-to-be-done research, behavioral segmentation and choice architecture, and it treats key assumptions as hypotheses to test. The result is a plan designed around real decision behavior, with leading indicators that show early whether it is working.

faqs.q: How long does this work take?
faqs.a: It depends on how much is already known and how quickly tests can run. Buyer research and segmentation can usually be completed in a matter of weeks. Market tests take longer because they need enough real responses to be meaningful. We scope the work so that useful decisions are possible at each stage rather than only at the end.

faqs.q: Do you only work on new product launches?
faqs.a: No. Many clients come to us when an existing product has stalled, when they are entering a new segment, or when founder-led sales need to become a repeatable motion. In those cases the work starts by understanding why current buyers chose the product and why others did not, which often reveals a sharper positioning.

faqs.q: How do you handle B2B buying committees?
faqs.a: We map the roles involved in a purchase, what each person needs to believe, and where decisions stall. Different stakeholders often weigh risk, cost and benefit differently. We design materials and sales steps that help a champion build internal consensus, since many B2B deals are lost to internal inertia rather than to a competitor.

services.name: Process Mapping & Improvement
services.meta_description: Process mapping that captures how work really flows: swimlanes, value stream maps and handoff analysis, plus the human behaviors that make processes stick.
services.summary: See how work actually flows across teams and systems, then redesign processes around the handoffs and human behaviors that determine performance.
services.lede: Process mapping is most valuable when it shows how work really happens, not how the policy manual says it should. We map the people, handoffs and decisions behind your processes and redesign them for performance people will sustain.
challenge: Most organizations have process documentation. Few have documentation that matches reality. Over time, workarounds accumulate, systems are added without being integrated, and informal handoffs replace formal ones. The result is delay, rework and errors that no single team owns. Leaders sense the problem in missed deadlines and frustrated customers but cannot see where it originates, because each team's view of the process ends at its own boundary. The cost is borne by staff and customers alike.

Traditional process improvement often focuses on steps and systems while overlooking behavior. Yet processes are performed by people who make judgment calls, avoid tasks they find unclear and route around steps they distrust. A redesigned process that ignores those behaviors tends to drift back to the old way within months. Effective process mapping captures both the formal flow and the human decisions within it, so improvements address the real causes of friction and are designed to be adopted, not merely announced.

approach.title: Walk the process in context
approach.body: We conduct contextual inquiry with the people who perform the work, observing tasks in real settings and following individual cases from start to finish. We capture the informal steps, workarounds and judgment calls that rarely appear in documentation, along with the frustrations that signal where the process is failing the people inside it.

approach.title: Quantify delay and rework
approach.body: We combine system timestamps, ticket and case data, and observation to measure cycle time, wait time, rework loops and handoff failure points. Value stream mapping separates value-adding work from waiting and duplication. The analysis identifies the few bottlenecks and decision points that drive most of the delay, which is where redesign effort should focus.

approach.title: Redesign flow and handoffs
approach.body: We create swimlane maps of the future-state process with explicit ownership, decision rights and information transfer at each handoff. We design for behavior as well as flow: clear prompts, simplified forms, sensible defaults and checklists at error-prone moments. Changes are prioritized by impact and by how easily the people doing the work can adopt them.

approach.title: Pilot and measure
approach.body: We pilot the redesigned process with one team, region or case type and track the same measures used in the baseline. We also gather feedback from the people performing the work, since their experience often reveals adjustments needed before wider rollout. Results inform a final design grounded in observed performance.

approach.title: Embed and sustain
approach.body: We support rollout with updated documentation, training, system configuration requirements and a dashboard of process health indicators. We coach process owners to run regular reviews and to treat the process as something that keeps improving. Clear ownership is what prevents the process from drifting back to old habits.

deliverables: Current-state swimlane maps based on direct observation
Value stream map with cycle time and wait-time analysis
Bottleneck and handoff failure analysis with root causes
Future-state process design with ownership and decision rights
Pilot plan, results and adoption feedback summary
Process health dashboard and owner review routine
outcomes: Teams share one accurate picture of how work flows across functions and systems
Handoffs carry clear ownership and the information the next person actually needs
Leaders can see bottlenecks and rework as they develop rather than after customers complain
Improved processes hold over time because they were designed around how people work
services.who_we_serve: We work with chief operating officers, operations and transformation leaders, heads of client service and department leaders in organizations where work crosses many teams and systems. Common triggers include growth that has outpaced informal processes, a merger or reorganization, a new technology platform, recurring customer complaints about delays, and regulatory or compliance pressure that requires consistent, documented processes. We also support nonprofits and public agencies.
services.impact_lens: Better processes make work more humane. Employees spend less time chasing information, redoing tasks and absorbing blame for failures they did not cause. Customers and patients experience fewer delays and errors. In mission-driven organizations, efficient processes free staff time for the people they serve. We involve frontline staff in redesign because they understand the work best and deserve a voice in how it changes.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a swimlane map and a value stream map?
faqs.a: A swimlane map shows who does what and when, with each role or team in its own lane, making handoffs and ownership visible. A value stream map focuses on flow and time, distinguishing value-adding work from waiting, rework and duplication. We often use both, since one clarifies accountability and the other reveals where time is lost.

faqs.q: Why include behavioral science in process mapping?
faqs.a: Processes are carried out by people who make choices. They skip steps they find unclear, create workarounds when systems are slow and avoid handoffs they do not trust. Process mapping that captures those behaviors leads to designs people will actually follow. Without that, improvements often look good on paper and fade within months.

faqs.q: Do you recommend technology changes?
faqs.a: When technology is part of the problem, yes. We document system requirements and integration gaps that the process redesign depends on. But we are technology-neutral and often find that clarifying ownership, simplifying steps and improving handoffs delivers meaningful gains before any new system is purchased. When new systems are warranted, a clear future-state process makes vendor selection and configuration far more effective.

faqs.q: How involved will our staff need to be?
faqs.a: Frontline involvement is essential. We need time with the people who do the work for observation and interviews, and we involve them in testing the redesigned process. We schedule this carefully to minimize disruption. Their participation also builds ownership, which is one of the strongest predictors that a new process will last.

services.name: Product Strategy & Development
services.meta_title: Product Strategy Consulting Grounded in User Behavior
services.meta_description: Product strategy consulting from former founders: jobs to be done research, behavioral evidence, prototyping and user testing to build products people adopt.
services.summary: Decide what to build and why, using jobs-to-be-done research, behavioral evidence and fast user testing from a team that has founded products.
services.lede: Our product strategy consulting is shaped by having founded and scaled software products ourselves. We help teams decide what to build by studying the behavior they need to change, then prototyping and testing before committing engineering time.
challenge: Product roadmaps fill up quickly. Sales relays customer requests, executives bring ideas from board meetings, engineers propose technical improvements and competitors ship features that feel urgent to match. Without a clear model of what users are trying to accomplish and which behaviors drive adoption and retention, prioritization becomes a negotiation. Teams ship steadily, yet the product grows more complex without becoming more valuable, and usage data shows features that few people touch.

We have lived this problem from the inside. We founded and scaled a research-dissemination platform built on social technology, and a website compliance archiving product for banks and dealerships, and learned that the hardest product questions are behavioral. Will people change an established habit to use this? What prompt will bring them back? What makes a compliance officer trust an automated record? We have also taught behavioral design, user testing and human-computer interaction, and we bring that discipline to the product strategy work we do for clients.

approach.title: Study jobs and workarounds
approach.body: We interview and observe current users, lapsed users and non-users to understand the jobs they are trying to get done, the workarounds they rely on today and the moments of frustration that create demand. Contextual inquiry often reveals that the most valuable opportunity is different from the most requested feature.

approach.title: Find the adoption behaviors
approach.body: We analyze product usage data to identify the activation moments and usage patterns that predict retention, and the behavioral types that use the product differently. This shows which capabilities create lasting value and which add complexity without changing behavior, giving the roadmap an evidence base rather than a list of requests.

approach.title: Prototype the critical moments
approach.body: We translate findings into product principles, prioritized opportunities and low-fidelity prototypes of the moments that matter most. Using behavioral design, we consider motivation, ability and prompts at each step, so that the product makes the desired behavior easier rather than relying on users to work harder.

approach.title: Test before building
approach.body: We run usability tests, concept tests and, where practical, painted-door or limited-release experiments to validate demand and usability before full engineering investment. Each test is tied to a specific hypothesis on the roadmap, and results determine whether an idea moves forward, changes shape or is set aside.

approach.title: Build a product discovery rhythm
approach.body: We help product teams adopt a lasting discovery practice: regular user conversations, a hypothesis backlog, adoption and retention metrics tied to behavior, and lightweight testing routines. We coach product leaders to make evidence visible in roadmap decisions, which also makes trade-offs easier to explain to executives and investors.

deliverables: Jobs-to-be-done research synthesis with opportunity map
Activation and retention behavior analysis from usage data
Product principles and prioritized opportunity backlog
Prototypes of critical user moments with design rationale
Usability and concept test results with recommendations
Product discovery playbook and behavior-based product metrics
outcomes: Roadmap decisions rest on evidence about user behavior rather than the loudest request
Teams validate demand and usability before committing significant engineering effort
Products become simpler to adopt because they are designed around real user jobs
Product leaders can explain priorities to executives and investors with clear behavioral evidence
services.who_we_serve: We work with founders, chief product officers, product managers and innovation leaders in software companies, digital health ventures, financial services firms and organizations building their first digital products. Common triggers include an early product searching for fit, a mature product with stalled adoption, a roadmap overloaded with competing requests, a pivot under consideration, or a new venture inside an established company that needs startup discipline.
services.impact_lens: Products designed around real human needs waste less of people's time and attention. Users benefit from tools that are easier to learn and that respect their goals instead of maximizing engagement for its own sake. Product teams benefit from clearer priorities and less wasted work. We are attentive to products that serve sensitive needs, such as health, money and learning, where good design can meaningfully improve people's lives.

faqs.q: What does product strategy consulting include?
faqs.a: It typically includes user research to understand jobs and behaviors, analysis of usage data to find what drives adoption and retention, prioritization of opportunities, prototyping and testing before development, and help establishing an ongoing discovery practice. The aim is a roadmap grounded in evidence and a team that can keep generating that evidence on its own.

faqs.q: How does behavioral science change product strategy?
faqs.a: It shifts the central question from what features to build to what behavior the product needs to enable. Models of motivation, ability and prompts help explain why users do or do not adopt a feature. Concepts like habit formation, defaults and friction guide design choices that make valuable behavior easier and more likely to repeat.

faqs.q: Do you build software?
faqs.a: We do not provide engineering teams. We work alongside your product and engineering staff, contributing research, strategy, behavioral design, prototypes and testing. Our founding experience means we understand engineering trade-offs and write recommendations that development teams can act on, but delivery stays with your team or chosen partners. We also review designs during development to keep critical behavioral moments intact.

faqs.q: Can you help an early-stage startup?
faqs.a: Yes. Early-stage companies often benefit most, because untested assumptions are cheapest to correct before they are built into the product and the sales story. We tailor the scope to the stage, focusing on the few questions that most affect product-market fit and the evidence investors will want to see. We have been in that position ourselves, which shapes how practical our advice is.

services.name: Customer Retention Strategy
services.meta_title: Customer Retention Strategy & Churn Reduction Consulting
services.meta_description: Customer retention strategy built on behavioral signals: find the early behaviors that predict churn, design timely interventions and test what keeps customers.
services.summary: Identify the early behaviors that predict churn, then design and test interventions that help customers keep getting value and choose to stay.
services.lede: An effective customer retention strategy acts before the cancellation notice arrives. We find the behavioral signals that precede churn, design interventions at those moments, and test which ones help customers keep getting value.
challenge: Most organizations learn that a customer is leaving when it is already decided. Cancellation surveys arrive after the fact, exit reasons are vague, and save offers at the last moment mainly teach customers that threatening to leave earns a discount. Meanwhile, the real story of disengagement started months earlier, in a missed onboarding step, a drop in usage, a service failure that went unresolved, or a renewal that arrived with no reminder of the value delivered.

Retention is behavioral long before it is financial. Cohort retention curves show when customers drift, but not why. Behavioral signals hidden in product usage, service tickets, payment patterns and engagement data can predict disengagement while there is still time to act. Psychological factors matter as well: habits that never formed, a sense that the product is not delivering its promise, or a competing offer framed more persuasively. A customer retention strategy that reads these signals can intervene with help instead of discounts.

approach.title: Listen to leavers and stayers
approach.body: We interview recently churned customers, at-risk customers and loyal long-term customers, and review service interactions and complaints. We reconstruct the path to disengagement and the reasons loyal customers stay. These stories often reveal that the stated reason for leaving, such as price, masks an earlier failure to realize value.

approach.title: Build churn early warnings
approach.body: We analyze cohort retention, usage, service, billing and engagement data to find the behaviors that precede churn and the milestones that predict long-term retention. We define behavioral types, such as customers who never activated and customers whose usage has quietly declined, and turn the strongest signals into predictive retention KPIs and early warning rules.

approach.title: Design timely interventions
approach.body: For each risk signal and segment, we design interventions matched to the underlying cause: onboarding support for customers who never activated, value reminders before renewal, service recovery after failures and habit-building prompts for lapsing users. We address loss aversion and status quo effects honestly, emphasizing value delivered rather than artificial switching barriers.

approach.title: Test with holdout groups
approach.body: We test interventions against holdout groups to measure their true effect on retention, since many customers would have stayed or left regardless. Tests run on the leading indicators first, such as re-engagement and milestone completion, so the organization learns quickly which interventions deserve broader investment and which can be dropped.

approach.title: Operationalize retention
approach.body: We integrate early warnings into the systems and routines customer success, service and marketing teams already use, with clear playbooks for each signal. A retention dashboard tracks leading and lagging indicators by cohort. We coach team leaders to review signals regularly so retention becomes an ongoing discipline rather than a quarterly emergency.

services.who_we_serve: We work with chief customer officers, customer success and marketing leaders, membership directors and general managers in subscription businesses, software companies, health clubs, financial services firms, associations and consumer brands. services.impact_lens: A good customer retention strategy keeps customers by helping them succeed, not by making it harder to leave. Customers benefit from timely support, clearer value and fewer unresolved problems. Employees in service and success roles benefit from focusing effort where it helps most. For associations and health clubs, retention often reflects real wellbeing and community outcomes. We advise against dark patterns such as obstructive cancellation flows, which damage trust and reputation.

faqs.q: What are behavioral signals of churn?
faqs.a: They are changes in what customers do that tend to precede leaving: declining logins or usage, abandoned onboarding steps, unresolved service tickets, skipped events, payment friction or reduced engagement with communications. The specific signals vary by business, so we identify them from your data and validate which ones actually predict churn in your customer base.

faqs.q: Is this a churn prediction model?
faqs.a: It can include one, but the goal is broader. A model that flags risk is useful only if teams know why a customer is at risk and what to do about it. We pair predictive signals with an understanding of causes and a tested set of interventions, so predictions translate into action rather than another unused report.

faqs.q: Why do you test retention efforts with holdout groups?
faqs.a: Without a comparison group, it is easy to credit an intervention for customers who would have stayed anyway. Holdout testing shows the true incremental effect, which helps leaders invest in efforts that work and stop those that only appear to. It also avoids rewarding offers that train customers to threaten cancellation.

faqs.q: How does retention connect to cohort analysis?
faqs.a: Cohort retention curves show how groups of customers acquired at the same time behave over their lifetime, revealing when drop-off happens and whether newer cohorts retain better than older ones. We combine cohort views with behavioral data to explain the shape of those curves and to find the milestones that separate customers who stay from those who leave.

services.name: Responsible AI Adoption
services.meta_title: Responsible AI Adoption Consulting for Organizations
services.meta_description: Responsible AI adoption consulting: learn how people really use AI tools, build trust and judgment, and weigh the cultures your training data leaves behind.
services.summary: Help people adopt AI tools with sound judgment and trust, while weighing the ethical, cultural and human consequences of how those systems are used.
services.lede: Responsible AI adoption is a behavioral challenge as much as a technical one. We help organizations understand how people actually use AI, design for calibrated trust and good judgment, and consider whose knowledge and culture those systems carry.
challenge: Many organizations have licensed AI tools and announced an AI strategy, yet usage remains uneven. Some employees avoid the tools entirely, wary of errors or of what adoption implies for their jobs. Others rely on them uncritically, pasting outputs into client work without verification. Leaders see adoption dashboards but not the quality of judgment behind each use. The gap between purchasing AI and using it well is fundamentally about human behavior, trust and organizational culture.

There is also a broader responsibility. AI systems learn from training material, and that material reflects some cultures, languages and bodies of knowledge far more than others. The choices organizations make about which tools to use, what data to contribute and how outputs shape decisions influence which perspectives get amplified and which get left behind. Responsible AI adoption means attending to fairness, transparency and the cultures we leave behind, not only to productivity and risk.

approach.title: See how AI is really used
approach.body: We interview and observe employees across roles as they use, avoid or work around AI tools. We document the tasks where AI helps, where it introduces risk and where people distrust it. We also explore concerns about job security, accountability and quality, since these shape behavior more than training materials do.

approach.title: Measure adoption and judgment
approach.body: We combine usage data with targeted surveys and work-sample reviews to understand not only how often tools are used but how well. We identify behavioral types, from cautious avoiders to over-reliant adopters, and define predictive indicators of healthy adoption, such as verification habits and appropriate escalation, rather than relying on raw usage counts.

approach.title: Design for calibrated trust
approach.body: We design workflows, prompts, guidelines and interface patterns that support calibrated trust: using AI where it is reliable, checking it where it is not and keeping humans accountable for consequential decisions. We address psychological safety so people can admit uncertainty, and we review training data and vendor choices for cultural and representational gaps.

approach.title: Pilot with real workflows
approach.body: We pilot new workflows and guidance with selected teams, comparing quality, efficiency and error patterns against current practice. We gather feedback on trust and workload, and we test whether the guidance actually changes verification and escalation behavior. Results show where AI adds value and where boundaries need to be tighter.

approach.title: Build responsible practice
approach.body: We help leaders roll out validated practices with role-specific training, governance routines, quality indicators and a feedback channel for problems. We coach leaders to model thoughtful AI use and to discuss trade-offs openly. The aim is a culture that adopts AI with confidence and keeps asking whether it serves people well.

services.impact_lens: Responsible AI adoption protects the people affected by AI-assisted decisions, from customers and patients to students and communities. Employees benefit from clear guidance, honest conversation about job impact and tools that support their expertise rather than undermine it. Society benefits when organizations consider the cultures, languages and knowledge represented in training material, helping ensure AI does not quietly erase perspectives that were already underrepresented.

faqs.q: What does responsible AI adoption mean in practice?
faqs.a: It means using AI where it genuinely helps, keeping humans accountable for consequential decisions, verifying outputs appropriately and being transparent with the people affected. It also means considering fairness and representation, including which cultures and knowledge the systems learn from. In practice that translates into workflows, guidelines, training and measures that shape everyday behavior.

faqs.q: Why treat AI adoption as a behavioral problem?
faqs.a: Because technology access does not determine how people use it. Trust, perceived competence, job security concerns, team norms and leadership signals all shape whether employees avoid AI, overuse it or use it well. Technology adoption research consistently shows that behavior, not availability, determines value. Treating adoption as behavior lets leaders design for good judgment rather than simply mandating use and hoping for the best.

faqs.q: Do you select or implement AI tools?
faqs.a: We are vendor-neutral and do not implement software. We help define the human requirements, evaluate how tools fit real workflows, review cultural and representational considerations and design the practices that make adoption work. Technical implementation stays with your technology team or chosen vendors. Independence from vendors lets us give candid advice about fit, limits and risks.

faqs.q: What do you mean by the cultures we leave behind?
faqs.a: AI systems learn from the material they are trained on, which overrepresents some languages, cultures and kinds of knowledge. As organizations rely more on these systems, perspectives absent from that material risk becoming less visible. We help organizations recognize this, make informed choices and, where possible, contribute to more representative knowledge.

services.name: Social Impact Strategy
services.meta_title: Social Impact Strategy Consulting with Behavioral Science
services.meta_description: Social impact strategy built on a clear theory of change: identify the behaviors that link programs to outcomes, then design, test and scale what works.
services.summary: Build a social impact strategy around the specific behaviors that connect your programs to better health, learning and community outcomes.
services.lede: A social impact strategy succeeds when people in the communities you serve actually do something differently. We help mission-driven organizations define those behaviors, build a theory of change around them, and invest where change is most likely.
challenge: Mission-driven organizations rarely lack purpose. They often lack a clear line between their activities and the change they exist to create. Programs accumulate over years, each with its own funder, reporting format and champion. Boards see activity counts: workshops held, materials distributed, people reached. What remains unclear is whether families are getting screened earlier, students are staying enrolled or patients are reaching care sooner. Without that clarity, resources spread thin and hard choices get postponed.

Behavioral science adds precision. Most social outcomes depend on specific behaviors by specific people: a parent scheduling a vaccination, a teacher adopting a new practice, a clinician referring to community mental health services, a resident trusting public health guidance. A social impact strategy built on a theory of change identifies those behaviors, the barriers that stand in the way and the evidence that the organization's work can move them. That focus helps leaders choose where to invest and what to stop.

approach.title: Listen to the community
approach.body: We conduct interviews and listening sessions with the people the organization serves, frontline staff, partners and funders. We seek to understand daily realities, barriers and assets in the community, and we give particular weight to voices that are often missing from strategy discussions, such as people who stopped participating or never engaged.

approach.title: Map behaviors to outcomes
approach.body: We review program data, public datasets and research evidence to build a theory of change and logic model that links activities to the specific behaviors, and then to the outcomes, the organization exists to improve. We identify which links are supported by evidence and which rest on assumptions that need testing.

approach.title: Choose focused strategies
approach.body: We help leadership prioritize the behaviors and populations where the organization can make the greatest difference, and design or refine programs to address the real barriers, whether motivation, ability, access, trust or timing. We also identify activities to stop or hand off, which is often the hardest and most valuable decision.

approach.title: Pilot and learn
approach.body: We design pilots with clear success measures and, where feasible, comparison groups. Pilots focus on the riskiest assumptions in the theory of change. We bring participants and frontline staff into the review of results, so adjustments reflect both the data and the lived experience of the community.

approach.title: Align the organization
approach.body: We translate the strategy into goals, indicators and a learning agenda that staff, boards and funders can share. We coach leaders to use the theory of change in budgeting and program decisions, and help them communicate the strategy to funders in terms of behaviors and outcomes rather than activity alone.

Priority behaviors and populations with barrier analysis

services.impact_lens: The purpose of social impact strategy is better lives: earlier diagnoses, children who stay in school, people who reach mental health care, communities that can trust and act on public health information. Staff benefit from clarity about why their work matters and permission to stop low-value activity. Funders benefit from honest evidence. We design with communities, not merely for them, and respect people's autonomy in every behavior we aim to support.

faqs.q: What is a theory of change?
faqs.a: A theory of change describes how and why an organization's activities are expected to lead to its intended outcomes, including the assumptions in between. A logic model is a structured version showing inputs, activities, outputs and outcomes. We add a behavioral layer, specifying which people need to do what differently, because outcomes depend on those behaviors.

faqs.q: How does behavioral science improve social impact strategy?
faqs.a: It clarifies the behaviors that drive outcomes and the barriers that prevent them, such as limited access, low trust, competing demands or a lack of timely prompts. Programs designed around those barriers tend to be more effective than programs designed around information alone, because knowing what to do is rarely the only obstacle.

faqs.q: Do you work with small nonprofits?
faqs.a: Yes. We scope work to fit the organization's resources, sometimes focusing on a single program or a facilitated theory of change process. Smaller organizations often benefit most from clarity, because limited resources make focus essential and every program decision carries more weight. Clear priorities also make smaller organizations more compelling to funders who want to understand exactly how their support creates change in the community.

faqs.q: How do you involve the communities being served?
faqs.a: We include community members in research from the start through interviews, listening sessions and participation in reviewing pilot results. We compensate participants fairly where appropriate and pay attention to accessibility, language and trust. Their insight regularly changes the strategy in ways leadership alone would not have anticipated. Engaging communities this way also builds the trust programs need to succeed.

services.meta_description: Nonprofit and association consulting grounded in behavioral science: member engagement, volunteer and donor behavior, programs and mission impact.
services.summary: Strengthen member engagement, volunteer participation and mission impact for associations and nonprofits, using behavioral research and practical program design.
services.lede: Our association consulting helps medical associations, public health associations and nonprofits understand what members, volunteers and donors actually do, then design engagement and programs that serve both the organization and the public good.
challenge: Associations and nonprofits depend on voluntary behavior. Members choose to renew, attend, volunteer and advocate. Donors choose to give again. Professionals choose to adopt the guidelines and education an association produces. Each of those choices competes with crowded calendars and other organizations asking for the same attention. Many associations see aging membership, uneven engagement among early-career professionals and programs that are well regarded but lightly used, without a clear picture of why.

For medical and public health associations, the stakes extend beyond the organization. When members adopt a new clinical guideline, complete continuing education or participate in public health advocacy, patients and communities benefit. When they do not, valuable knowledge stays on the shelf. Association consulting grounded in behavioral science helps leaders see membership as a set of behaviors with identifiable drivers, and design value, communication and programs that make the most important behaviors easier and more rewarding.

approach.title: Understand member lives
approach.body: We interview members at different career stages, lapsed members, volunteers, donors and staff, exploring what professional problems they face and where the association fits. We look for the moments when membership feels essential and the moments when it fades from view, as well as barriers such as time, cost and relevance.

approach.title: Read engagement data
approach.body: We analyze membership, event, learning, giving and communication data to identify behavioral types and the engagement patterns that predict renewal, volunteering and continued giving. Many associations hold years of untapped data across separate systems. Integrating it often reveals early signals, such as first-year participation, that predict long-term commitment.

approach.title: Design value and engagement
approach.body: We design member journeys, onboarding, communications and program changes matched to each behavioral type. approach.title: Test engagement changes
approach.body: We test communication variants, onboarding sequences, event formats and renewal approaches with controlled comparisons where possible. Tests focus on leading indicators such as first-year participation and volunteer activation, giving leadership timely evidence on what deepens engagement and what does not before committing broader resources. approach.title: Build engagement capability
approach.body: We help staff adopt engagement dashboards, testing routines and member research practices, and we advise boards and executives on governance of member data and strategy. Coaching helps leaders sustain a culture of learning from member behavior rather than relying on annual surveys alone. Over time, engagement insight also informs advocacy, education and the association's public mission.

faqs.q: Do you work with medical and public health associations specifically?
faqs.a: Yes. Our roots in clinical and health psychology and behavioral medicine make us comfortable with clinical audiences, continuing education and guideline adoption. faqs.q: How do you handle sensitive member data?

services.name: Education & Learning Design
services.meta_title: Learning Design Consulting Grounded in Behavioral Science
services.meta_description: Learning design consulting for schools, universities, associations and employers: adult learning, behavior change and evaluation built into every program.
services.summary: Design courses and learning programs that change what people actually do, grounded in adult learning principles, behavioral science and real evaluation.
services.lede: Effective learning design measures success by what learners do afterward, not by completion rates. We draw on adult learning, behavioral science and years of university teaching to build programs that change practice in classrooms, clinics and workplaces.
challenge: Organizations invest heavily in education and training, yet much of it fails to change behavior. Continuing education courses are completed for credit and forgotten. Professional development days leave teachers inspired on Friday and back to old routines on Monday. Online modules produce completion certificates without new practice. The underlying issue is that many programs are designed to transfer information, while the real goal is a change in what people do under real conditions, with competing demands and limited time.

We have taught behavioral design, user testing, human-computer interaction and data visualization at a design institute, and we bring both classroom experience and behavioral science to learning design. Adult learners need relevance, autonomy and the chance to apply new skills to their own problems. Habits change through practice, feedback and prompts in context. Learning design that respects these principles, and that is evaluated by changes in practice, produces programs that matter to learners and to the people they serve.

approach.title: Understand learners at work
approach.body: We interview and observe learners in their real settings, whether classrooms, clinics or offices, to understand what they need to do differently and what makes it hard. We also speak with supervisors, students or patients who are affected by that practice, since they help define what better performance looks like.

approach.title: Define target behaviors
approach.body: We review existing learning data, assessments and performance indicators, and work with stakeholders to specify the target behaviors a program should change. Each behavior gets an observable definition and a way to measure it. This step often shows that existing programs teach knowledge that is not the real barrier to performance.

approach.title: Build for application
approach.body: We design curricula, activities and materials using adult learning principles: problem-centered content, active practice, spaced retrieval, peer learning and feedback. We build in prompts and supports that carry learning into daily work, such as job aids, follow-up challenges and coaching conversations, so new skills have a chance to become habits.

approach.title: Pilot and evaluate
approach.body: We pilot programs with a representative group of learners, testing usability, engagement and early application. Evaluation design looks beyond satisfaction surveys to measure learning, application and, where possible, effects on outcomes. Findings drive revisions before broader rollout, so the full launch reflects what learners actually need.

approach.title: Equip educators to sustain it
approach.body: We prepare facilitators, faculty and instructional teams to deliver and adapt the program, with facilitator guides, measurement tools and a review cycle. We coach program leaders to use evaluation evidence in ongoing decisions, so programs improve over time instead of being repeated unchanged year after year.

services.impact_lens: Learning that changes practice has effects far beyond the classroom. When teachers adopt better instructional practices, students learn more. faqs.q: What is behavior-focused learning design?
faqs.a: It starts by defining what learners should do differently and designs everything around enabling and sustaining that behavior. Content is chosen for relevance, practice and feedback are central, and supports extend into the workplace or classroom. Evaluation measures application, not only knowledge or satisfaction. This approach treats a course as the beginning of a change in practice rather than the end of a requirement.

faqs.q: What are adult learning principles?
faqs.a: Adults learn best when content is relevant to their current problems, when they have autonomy in how they engage, when they can draw on their experience and when they can apply new skills immediately. These principles, along with spaced practice and retrieval, guide how we structure programs for professionals. Ignoring them is one of the most common reasons professional learning fails to change practice.

faqs.q: Do you design K-12 student curricula?
faqs.a: Our education work focuses mostly on educators, school leaders, district initiatives and family engagement, as well as higher education and professional learning. We collaborate with curriculum specialists when student-facing materials are needed, contributing behavioral science, research and evaluation design to their content expertise. For districts, we also support family engagement and communication efforts that help students attend, participate and succeed.

faqs.q: How do you evaluate whether learning worked?
faqs.a: We design evaluation at the start, measuring reactions, learning, application and, where feasible, outcomes. Methods include pre and post assessments, observation, self and supervisor reports, follow-up surveys and performance data. Comparison groups strengthen conclusions when they can be arranged ethically and practically. Findings are reported in plain language so educators can act on them in the next cycle.

services.name: Research Translation & Knowledge Dissemination
services.meta_description: Research translation that makes scientific knowledge accessible: knowledge translation strategy, plain-language design and dissemination tested with audiences.
services.summary: Make scientific knowledge accessible and usable for clinicians, educators, policymakers and the public, through tested knowledge translation and dissemination strategies.
services.lede: Research translation turns findings into knowledge people can understand and act on. We help researchers, academic medical centers and associations design and test dissemination that reaches clinicians, educators, policymakers and the public.
challenge: Valuable research too often reaches only other researchers. Findings appear in journals behind paywalls, written for specialists, while the clinicians, teachers, community leaders and patients who could use them never encounter them or cannot interpret them. The research-to-practice gap is well documented and costly. Evidence that could improve care, learning or public policy waits years to be adopted, and public trust in science suffers when people encounter it mostly through oversimplified headlines.

We have worked on this problem from several directions. We founded a research-dissemination platform built on social technology, designed to help scientific knowledge travel beyond academic circles. We have taught data visualization and behavioral design. We have studied how audiences interpret evidence. Effective research translation requires understanding what specific audiences need, how they make decisions, which formats and messengers they trust, and how to communicate uncertainty honestly. It is a design and behavior problem, not only a writing problem.

approach.title: Understand knowledge users
approach.body: We interview the people who should benefit from the research, such as clinicians, teachers, policymakers, patients or community members, to learn how they currently find and use evidence, what decisions they face and what they trust. This defines the audience's real questions, which are often different from the questions researchers expect.

approach.title: Find what travels
approach.body: We analyze existing dissemination data, such as downloads, citations in practice documents, media coverage and engagement across channels, to see which formats and messengers reach each audience. We also identify the key findings with the greatest practical relevance and the behaviors the research should inform.

approach.title: Translate and visualize
approach.body: We create knowledge translation products tailored to each audience: plain-language summaries, decision aids, visual explainers, data visualizations, practice briefs and toolkits. We apply clear framing, careful communication of uncertainty and accessible design for varied literacy levels, while keeping scientific accuracy intact through close collaboration with researchers.

approach.title: Test comprehension and use
approach.body: We test materials with members of each audience for comprehension, trust and intended use, and we compare formats where appropriate. Testing frequently reveals misunderstandings that experts cannot see in their own writing. Revisions continue until audiences can accurately explain the finding and what it means for their decisions.

approach.title: Build dissemination capacity
approach.body: We help research teams and organizations build a repeatable dissemination strategy, with partner channels, trusted messengers, templates, measurement of reach and use, and training for researchers. The goal is a sustainable practice of knowledge translation that becomes part of every project rather than an afterthought at its end.

Dissemination reach and channel analysis
Knowledge translation strategy by audience
Plain-language summaries, visual explainers and practice briefs
Comprehension and usability test results

Audiences understand findings accurately, including what remains uncertain and what it means for them
