Public trust grows when people encounter science that is clear, honest and relevant
services.who_we_serve: We work with research centers, academic medical centers, university faculty and communications offices, foundations that fund research, medical and public health associations, and government or nonprofit agencies responsible for evidence-based guidance. Common triggers include a funder dissemination requirement, a major study nearing publication, a new practice guideline, low uptake of existing evidence, or a goal to rebuild public trust in a field.
services.impact_lens: Making scientific knowledge accessible is a public good in its own right. When research reaches practice, patients receive better care, students benefit from better teaching and policymakers decide with better evidence. Communities historically excluded from research deserve access to its findings in forms they can use. Researchers also benefit when their work has visible influence. We treat accuracy and honest uncertainty as ethical commitments, never sacrificed for reach.

faqs.q: What is knowledge translation?
faqs.a: Knowledge translation is the process of moving research findings into practice and public understanding through synthesis, dissemination, exchange and application. It goes beyond publishing to consider who needs the knowledge, how they make decisions and what formats, messengers and supports help them use it. Research translation is the practical work of making that happen.

faqs.q: How do you keep translated research accurate?
faqs.a: We work closely with the researchers throughout, review every claim against the source, and communicate uncertainty and limitations clearly rather than hiding them. Plain language does not mean oversimplification. Testing with audiences also checks whether readers come away with an accurate understanding, not just a positive impression. Where findings are preliminary or contested, we say so plainly and explain what that means for decisions.

faqs.q: Can you help meet funder dissemination requirements?
faqs.a: Yes. Many funders now expect dissemination and engagement plans. We help design plans that go beyond publishing, define audiences and channels, produce materials and measure reach and use. That strengthens future funding applications and demonstrates the practical value of the research. It also helps researchers describe the public value of their work to institutions and communities.

faqs.q: What role does data visualization play?
faqs.a: A significant one. Well-designed visualizations can make patterns, risks and comparisons understandable far faster than text, while poorly designed ones mislead. We apply visualization principles carefully, choose formats suited to each audience and test them for accurate interpretation, particularly when communicating risk and uncertainty to the public. Accessible visual design also helps readers with limited time or limited familiarity with statistics.

services.name: Public Awareness & Education Campaigns
services.meta_title: Public Awareness Campaign Strategy Grounded in Science
services.meta_description: Public awareness campaigns grounded in behavioral science: research the perception gap, frame messages ethically and test what changes understanding and action.
services.summary: Ground public awareness and education campaigns in research on what people believe, then frame and test messages that change understanding and action.
services.lede: A public awareness campaign should change what people understand and do, not just how many see it. We research the gap between evidence and public perception, design ethical messages, and test them before launch.
challenge: Public education campaigns often begin with a creative concept rather than an understanding of the audience. Organizations know their message is important, so they assume visibility will lead to understanding and action. But awareness alone rarely changes behavior. People filter information through existing beliefs, trusted sources and practical constraints. A campaign that ignores those filters may reach millions of people and change very little, or worse, reinforce misconceptions by repeating them.

We have researched the gap between an industry's real benefits and consumer perception specifically to ground an education campaign in science. That work showed how much campaigns depend on understanding which beliefs block action, which messengers are trusted and how framing affects interpretation. Public health and education campaigns face the same challenges with higher stakes. A public awareness campaign grounded in behavioral science targets the beliefs and barriers that matter, uses honest framing and builds in evaluation from the start.

approach.title: Research public understanding
approach.body: We conduct interviews and community conversations to learn what people currently believe about the issue, which sources they trust, what language they use and what practical barriers stand between awareness and action. We include groups the campaign most needs to reach, which are often the hardest to hear from through conventional research.

approach.title: Measure the perception gap
approach.body: We design surveys that measure knowledge, beliefs, attitudes, trust and intentions, and combine them with existing public data. Analysis identifies which beliefs most strongly predict the target behavior and which audience segments hold them. This shows where a campaign can make a meaningful difference and where other interventions, such as improved access, are needed.

approach.title: Frame messages ethically
approach.body: We develop message strategies and creative briefs grounded in research: framing that is honest and relevant, trusted messengers, social proof that reflects real norms, concrete calls to action and attention to literacy and language. We avoid fear tactics that backfire and messages that inadvertently spread the misconceptions they aim to correct.

approach.title: Pretest with real audiences
approach.body: We pretest messages and materials with members of target audiences, measuring comprehension, credibility, emotional response and intended action, and comparing variants through randomized tests where possible. Pretesting catches confusion, unintended interpretations and cultural missteps before they reach the public, when changes are still inexpensive. Community partners help interpret the results.

approach.title: Launch and evaluate
approach.body: We support launch with an evaluation plan that tracks reach, understanding and behavior over time, ideally with comparison regions or groups. We help teams monitor early indicators and adjust channels and messages during the campaign, and we document lessons for future campaigns and partner organizations.

deliverables: Public understanding research with key misconceptions and barriers
Perception gap survey and segment analysis
Message strategy and research-based creative brief
Pretest results comparing message and material variants
Campaign evaluation plan with behavioral indicators
Campaign learning report for partners and funders
outcomes: Campaigns target the specific beliefs and barriers that stand between awareness and action
Messages are understood as intended across audiences with different backgrounds and literacy levels
Organizations avoid campaign approaches that backfire or reinforce existing misconceptions
Funders and leaders see evidence of changed understanding and behavior, not only reach
services.who_we_serve: We work with communications and program leaders at public health associations, medical associations, health departments, school districts, foundations, trade associations and nonprofits planning public education efforts. Common triggers include a new public health priority, an industry facing misunderstanding, low uptake of a beneficial service, a funded awareness initiative, or a campaign that achieved wide visibility without the behavior change it intended.
services.impact_lens: Well-designed public education helps people make informed decisions about their health, their children's learning and their communities. Accurate understanding can lead to earlier screening, better use of available services and more trust in reliable information. We are committed to campaigns that respect autonomy and avoid manipulation or stigma, especially for communities that have reasons to distrust institutions. Honest persuasion builds trust that lasts beyond any single campaign.

faqs.q: Why do awareness campaigns often fail to change behavior?
faqs.a: Awareness is rarely the only barrier. People may know what to do but lack time, access, trust or a clear next step. Campaigns that focus only on visibility miss those barriers. Grounding a public awareness campaign in research identifies what actually stands in the way, so messaging and complementary actions address the real problem.

faqs.q: Do fear-based messages work?
faqs.a: Fear can draw attention, but it often backfires when people do not feel able to act, leading to avoidance or denial. Research in health communication suggests threat messages work best, if at all, when paired with a clear, achievable action. We generally favor honest framing that builds confidence and relevance.

faqs.q: How do you test campaign messages?
faqs.a: We pretest with members of the target audience using interviews, surveys and randomized comparisons of message variants. We measure comprehension, credibility, emotional response and intended action. Where possible, we run small live tests in digital channels to observe real behavior before committing the full campaign budget. Testing with communities most affected also helps prevent messages that stigmatize or alienate the people a campaign needs to reach.

faqs.q: Can you work with our creative agency?
faqs.a: Yes. We typically supply the research, message strategy, creative brief and testing, while agencies develop creative execution and media plans. Collaboration from the start works best, so creative teams understand the audience insights and testing results feed directly into revisions. We can also help brief partner organizations who will carry the campaign into their own communities.

services.name: Community Behavioral Health Advisory
services.meta_title: Community Behavioral Health Consulting and Advisory
services.meta_description: Community behavioral health consulting: improve access, engagement and continuity of mental health care with behavioral research, service design and evaluation.
services.summary: Help community mental health organizations improve access, engagement and continuity of care, using behavioral research, service design and practical evaluation.
services.lede: Our community behavioral health consulting helps mental health and substance use providers reduce the barriers between people and care, from first contact to ongoing treatment, using behavioral science, service design and honest measurement.
challenge: Community behavioral health organizations serve people at difficult moments, often with limited funding, staffing shortages and complex reimbursement rules. Many people who reach out never complete intake. Others miss early appointments and disengage before treatment can help. Referrals from schools, primary care and hospitals are lost in transition. Staff work hard to fill gaps, but the system itself makes it difficult for people in distress to take each necessary step.

These are behavioral and design problems as much as resource problems. Stigma, fear, competing responsibilities and confusing processes all stand in the way of care. Waiting periods weaken motivation at the very moment it is highest. Clinicians and care coordinators face burnout that affects engagement. Our roots in clinical and health psychology and behavioral medicine shape how we approach this work, with respect for clinical judgment, lived experience and the realities of community settings.

approach.title: Walk the path to care
approach.body: We interview people who have sought care, family members, peer specialists, clinicians, intake staff and referral partners. We map the path from first contact through intake and early treatment, noting where people hesitate, wait, feel confused or feel judged. Lived experience is central to this research, and we handle it with care and confidentiality.

approach.title: Find where people drop off
approach.body: Using intake, scheduling, electronic health record and referral data, we measure conversion from inquiry to intake, intake to first session and early session attendance. We identify the drop-off points and the early behaviors that predict ongoing engagement, and we look for differences across populations that may indicate equity gaps in access.

approach.title: Redesign access and engagement
approach.body: We co-design improvements with staff and people with lived experience: simplified intake, warm handoffs from referral partners, reminders and outreach timed to reduce missed appointments, bridging support during waits, and language that reduces stigma. Service blueprints clarify roles so improvements fit staff capacity rather than adding to burnout.

approach.title: Pilot practical changes
approach.body: We pilot changes in a single program or site, measuring effects on intake completion, attendance and experience. We monitor staff workload as well, since changes that exhaust teams will not last. Results guide refinement, and we document what works in forms that are useful for grant reporting and funder conversations.

approach.title: Sustain and share
approach.body: We help leadership expand successful changes, build access and engagement dashboards, and coach supervisors to maintain improvements. We also help organizations communicate results to funders, partners and county or state agencies, strengthening the case for sustained investment in community mental health. Lessons are documented so peer organizations in the region can adapt them for their own communities.

deliverables: Path-to-care research including lived experience perspectives
Access funnel analysis from inquiry through early treatment
Equity review of access and engagement differences
Co-designed intake, handoff and engagement improvements
Service blueprint clarifying staff roles and capacity
Access dashboard and pilot results for funders
outcomes: More people who reach out for help successfully complete intake and begin care
Referrals from schools, primary care and hospitals arrive with warm, reliable handoffs
Staff spend less time compensating for broken processes and more time supporting clients
Leaders and funders can see where access improves and where equity gaps remain
services.who_we_serve: We work with executive directors, clinical and operations leaders, quality improvement teams and boards of community mental health centers, substance use treatment providers, certified community behavioral health clinics, school-based mental health programs and the agencies and foundations that fund them. Triggers include long waitlists, high no-show rates, a new funding or certification requirement, a crisis services expansion, or partnerships with schools and primary care.
services.impact_lens: Every step removed from the path to care can mean someone receives help sooner. Better access and engagement in community behavioral health can affect wellbeing, family stability, school success and safety. Staff benefit from processes that reduce frustration and burnout. We design with people who have lived experience, protect privacy rigorously and avoid approaches that pressure or stigmatize. Behavioral science here must serve autonomy and dignity first.

faqs.q: What does community behavioral health consulting involve?
faqs.a: It typically involves research with clients, staff and referral partners, analysis of access and engagement data, co-design of process improvements, pilot testing and support for sustained implementation. The focus is on reducing barriers to care and improving engagement while respecting clinical expertise, staff capacity and the dignity of the people being served.

faqs.q: Do you provide clinical services?
faqs.a: No. We are advisors, not a treatment provider. Our background in clinical and health psychology and behavioral medicine informs our work, but clinical decisions remain with your licensed professionals. We focus on access, engagement, processes, communication and measurement around clinical care. We collaborate closely with clinical leaders so every recommendation fits clinical standards, supervision structures and the needs of the people in care.

faqs.q: How do you protect client privacy?
faqs.a: We work within your privacy and compliance policies and applicable regulations, use de-identified data whenever possible and limit access to sensitive information. Interviews with people who have used services are voluntary, confidential and conducted with informed consent, with attention to trauma-informed practice. Participants can decline or stop at any time without any effect on their care.

faqs.q: Can this help with no-show rates?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Missed appointments usually reflect practical barriers, ambivalence or long waits rather than lack of interest. We identify the causes in your setting and test interventions such as well-timed reminders, shorter waits for first appointments, bridging contact and simpler rescheduling, measuring which ones actually improve attendance. Each improvement we test is judged by whether more people actually receive the help they sought.

services.name: Behavioral Science Workshops & Training
services.meta_title: Behavioral Science Training & Workshops for Teams
services.meta_description: Behavioral science training for leaders, product teams, educators and nonprofits: practical workshops on behavioral design, testing, measurement and ethics.
services.summary: Practical workshops that teach teams to apply behavioral design, user testing, measurement and ethical persuasion to their own real challenges.
services.lede: Our behavioral science training is built on years of university teaching in behavioral design, user testing, HCI and data visualization. Teams leave with practical methods applied to their own challenges, not just interesting theory.
challenge: Interest in behavioral science is widespread, but practical skill is rare. Many people have read popular books about nudges and biases, yet struggle to apply the ideas to a real product, program or campaign. Without method, behavioral science becomes a collection of anecdotes and clever tricks. Teams may copy tactics that worked elsewhere without understanding why, or overlook the ethical questions that arise whenever an organization deliberately shapes behavior. Skill requires structured practice.

Mission-driven organizations face an additional constraint. They often cannot afford ongoing consulting for every project, so building internal capability is the most sustainable way to apply behavioral science to public health, education and community programs. Effective behavioral science training must therefore be practical, grounded in sound methods and adapted to the participants' world. It should teach people to diagnose behavior, design interventions, test them honestly and use persuasion responsibly. Capability compounds over time.

approach.title: Learn the participants' context
approach.body: Before designing a workshop, we interview a sample of participants and sponsors about their work, current challenges and familiarity with behavioral science. We collect real examples, such as a stalled program or an underused feature, to serve as working cases, so the training addresses problems participants actually face.

approach.title: Set learning objectives
approach.body: We define the specific skills and behaviors participants should demonstrate afterward, such as writing a testable behavioral hypothesis, mapping a behavior with a motivation, ability and prompt lens, or designing a simple A/B test. Clear objectives shape the agenda and give sponsors a basis for evaluating whether the training succeeded.

approach.title: Build an applied curriculum
approach.body: We design interactive sessions combining concise explanation, examples from relevant sectors, structured exercises and work on participants' own cases. Topics can include behavior models, choice architecture, user testing, survey design, data visualization, experimentation and the ethics of persuasion. Adult learning principles guide pacing, practice and reflection.

approach.title: Practice and get feedback
approach.body: Participants apply methods during the workshop, receive feedback from facilitators and peers, and leave with a plan to test an idea in their work. Where programs run over several sessions, participants return with results to discuss. We evaluate the training against its objectives and refine future sessions accordingly.

approach.title: Build lasting capability
approach.body: We provide toolkits, templates and reference guides, and we can train internal champions to lead future sessions. Follow-up coaching helps teams apply methods to new projects. The goal is an organization that uses behavioral science routinely and responsibly rather than relying on a single memorable event.

Learning objectives aligned to sponsor goals
Custom workshop agenda, slides and exercises
Behavioral design and testing toolkit with templates

outcomes: Participants can diagnose behavior problems and write testable hypotheses about them

services.who_we_serve: We train leadership teams, product and marketing groups, program staff at nonprofits and associations, public health professionals, educators and administrators in school districts and universities, and clinician leaders in academic medicine. Common triggers include launching a behavioral science or innovation function, an annual meeting or retreat, a new strategy that depends on behavior change, or a desire to build internal capacity for testing and evaluation.
services.impact_lens: Behavioral science training multiplies impact when it reaches the people who design programs, products and services every day. Nonprofit and public sector staff can apply these methods to improve access, learning and health without large budgets. Employees gain skills that strengthen their careers. We always include the ethics of persuasion, so participants learn to help people achieve their own goals and to recognize and avoid manipulative practices.

faqs.q: What topics can behavioral science training cover?
faqs.a: Common topics include models of behavior and motivation, choice architecture and nudges, behavioral research and user testing, survey and measurement design, experimentation and A/B testing, data visualization, behavior change in teams and the ethics of persuasion. We tailor the mix to participants' roles and the problems they need to solve.

faqs.q: How long are the workshops?
faqs.a: Formats range from a focused session at a conference or retreat to multi-session programs over several weeks. Shorter sessions build awareness and shared vocabulary. Longer programs give participants time to apply methods to real projects and return with results, which builds practical capability more reliably. We recommend a format after understanding your goals, schedule and the participants' existing experience.

faqs.q: Can you speak at our annual meeting or conference?
faqs.a: Yes. We deliver keynotes and interactive sessions for associations, professional societies and organizational gatherings. We prefer formats that include some participation, even in large groups, because people retain more when they apply an idea to their own work immediately. Sessions for mission-driven audiences often focus on applying behavioral science to access, learning and public health challenges participants face every week.

faqs.q: Is the training suitable for people without a research background?
faqs.a: Yes. We design for practitioners, not specialists, and introduce methods in plain language with practical examples. Participants with research backgrounds can go deeper through advanced exercises. Mixed groups often work well, because they combine field knowledge with methodological skill. Shared language across these roles is often one of the most lasting benefits of the training.

services.name: Impact Measurement & Evaluation
services.meta_description: Impact measurement and program evaluation built on logic models, behavioral indicators and practical evaluation design that boards, staff and funders can trust.
services.summary: Measure whether programs are changing behavior and outcomes, with logic models, behavioral indicators and evaluation designs suited to real-world constraints.
services.lede: Impact measurement should tell you whether your work is changing people's lives and why. We build logic models, define behavioral indicators and design practical evaluations that boards, staff and funders can trust and use.
challenge: Mission-driven organizations are asked to prove impact constantly, yet the measures available are often weak. Reports count participants, sessions and satisfaction ratings because those are easy to collect. Funders request different metrics in different formats. Staff spend hours on data entry that never informs decisions. Meanwhile, the questions that matter most remain unanswered: Are participants actually doing something differently? Which parts of the program drive change? For whom does it work, and for whom does it not?

Rigorous evaluation can seem out of reach, especially for organizations without research staff. But useful impact measurement does not always require a large randomized trial. It requires a clear theory of change, indicators that capture behavior and outcomes, measures with sound psychometric properties and an evaluation design matched to the organization's resources and the decisions it needs to make. Our background in research methods, psychometrics and test-and-measurement shapes how we approach this work.

approach.title: Clarify questions and context
approach.body: We meet with leaders, staff, participants and funders to understand what each needs to learn and what decisions evaluation should inform. We review current data collection, reporting burdens and program delivery, observing the program where possible, so the evaluation fits real operations rather than an idealized version of them.

approach.title: Define behavioral indicators
approach.body: We build or refine the logic model and theory of change, then define indicators at each level: activities, participant behaviors and outcomes. We prioritize leading indicators of behavior change that show progress before long-term outcomes appear, and we assess existing data and measures for reliability, validity and usefulness.

approach.title: Design the evaluation
approach.body: We select evaluation designs suited to the questions and constraints, such as pre and post comparisons, comparison groups, staggered rollouts, mixed methods or, where feasible, randomized designs. We develop or adapt validated instruments, data collection protocols and analysis plans, and we reduce reporting burden by removing measures that do not inform decisions.

approach.title: Field and analyze
approach.body: We pilot instruments and protocols, refine them, then support data collection and conduct analysis. Findings address what changed, for whom and why, combining quantitative results with participant and staff perspectives. We report honestly, including null or mixed results, since those findings are essential for improving programs.

approach.title: Build a learning system
approach.body: We create dashboards and reporting templates aligned to the logic model and help organizations integrate evaluation into regular decisions. We coach staff to interpret data and adjust programs, and we help leaders communicate findings to boards and funders with clarity and integrity. Findings are also shared back with participants and communities where appropriate.

Logic model and theory of change with behavioral indicators
Measurement review with psychometric assessment of instruments
Evaluation design, protocols and analysis plan
Evaluation findings report with practical recommendations
Impact dashboard and funder reporting templates
outcomes: Organizations know whether programs are changing behavior and outcomes, not only attendance
Staff spend less time on reporting that never informs decisions
Boards and funders receive honest, credible evidence about what works and for whom
Programs improve continuously because evaluation findings feed directly into planning
services.who_we_serve: We work with executive directors, program and evaluation leaders, boards and funders of public health associations, medical associations, academic medicine programs, school districts, community mental health organizations, foundations and impact investors. Common triggers include a funder evaluation requirement, a program expansion decision, a strategic plan, a grant application that needs a stronger evaluation plan, or doubts about whether a long-running program still works.
services.impact_lens: Honest impact measurement protects the people programs are meant to serve. It helps organizations continue what works, fix what does not and direct scarce resources toward real benefit. Participants deserve programs that are effective, and their time and data should be respected in every survey and interview. Funders and the public gain credible evidence. Staff gain the satisfaction of knowing their effort makes a demonstrable difference.

faqs.q: What is the difference between impact measurement and program evaluation?
faqs.a: Impact measurement usually refers to ongoing tracking of outcomes and indicators. Program evaluation is a more focused assessment of whether and how a program works, often answering specific questions with a defined design. Both depend on a clear logic model and good measures, and the strongest organizations combine routine measurement with periodic evaluation.

faqs.q: Do we need a randomized controlled trial?
faqs.a: Not always. Randomized designs provide strong evidence but are not always feasible or ethical. Comparison groups, staggered rollouts, pre and post designs with careful controls and mixed methods can produce credible, useful evidence. We match the design to your questions, resources and the decisions the evidence must support. We are candid about the strength of evidence each design can provide, so findings are not overstated to funders or the public.

faqs.q: Why focus on behavioral indicators?
faqs.a: Long-term outcomes such as health status or graduation take time to change and are influenced by many factors. Behaviors that lead to those outcomes, such as screening, attendance or practice adoption, change sooner and are more directly tied to the program. Tracking them provides earlier and more actionable evidence of progress.

faqs.q: Can you help reduce our reporting burden?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. Many organizations collect data that no one uses. By aligning measures to the logic model and the decisions that matter, we often recommend dropping redundant items, consolidating instruments and creating shared reporting templates that satisfy several funders at once. Lighter reporting also respects participants, who should not answer questions that serve no purpose.
